passages.heading: **Results**
passages.text:
The baseline characteristics of the participants are shown in Table 1. A total of 770 (8.7%) of the participants were living with sarcopenia. The mean age of the participants was 39.2 years, and nearly half of the participants (50.4%) were female. A total of 36.8% of the participants were non-Hispanic white. The majority of the participants (83.5%) had a high school education or above, and more than half were married (59.7%). Figure 2 shows the differences in METs across different characteristics between the participants with and without sarcopenia. Total METs, METs for moderate-intensity PA, and METs for vigorous-intensity PA were significantly greater in the non-sarcopenia group than in the sarcopenia group (Fig. 2A-C). After stratification by occupation, the comparison of the METs for recreational PAs between sarcopenia patients and non-sarcopenia patients was similar to the results without stratification (Fig. 2G-I). However, there were no significant differences in total METs for occupational PA or METs for occupational vigorous-intensity PA across the groups of participants with and without sarcopenia (Fig. 2D and F). The cross-sectional associations between different intensities of PA (total, moderate, and vigorous) and sarcopenia are presented in Table 2. In the fully adjusted model, compared to participants without PAs (METs were 0), participants in the “low”, “moderate”, and “high” total METs groups had lower risks of sarcopenia (low: OR = 0.730, 95% CI: 0.583; 0.915, _p_ -value = 0.006; moderate: OR = 0.643, 95% CI: 0.485; 0.853, _p_ -value = 0.002; high: OR = 0.560; 95% CI: 0.457; 0.687, _p_ -value < 0.001). The stratified analysis of the associations between moderate- or vigorous-intensity METs and sarcopenia also yielded results similar to those of the non-stratified analysis. Table 3 shows the association between the intensity of occupational and recreational PA and sarcopenia. According to the fully adjusted model, the participants in the “high” total METs group had a significantly lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.789; 95% CI = 0.653; 0.954; _p_ -value = 0.014). Similarly, “high” METs for moderate-intensity occupational PA were associated with a lower risk of sarcopenia (high: OR = 0.797, 95% CI: 0.649; 0.980, _p_ -value = 0.031); however, higher METs for vigorous-intensity occupational PA were not associated with sarcopenia compared to the reference group. A higher intensity of recreational PA was associated with a lower risk of sarcopenia, i.e., the participants who were labeled with “low”, “moderate” and “high” total METs for recreational PA had a decreased risk of sarcopenia (low: OR = 0.758, 95% CI: 0.623; 0.921, _p_ -value = 0.005; moderate: OR = 0.725, 95% CI: 0.553; 0.950, _p_ -value = 0.020; high: OR = 0.444, 95% CI: 0.327; 0.604, _p_ -value < 0.001) compared to the reference group. Figure 3 shows the dose-response relationships between different categories of PA intensity and sarcopenia. The relationships between total METs, vigorous-intensity METs and sarcopenia showed a nonlinear U-shaped trend (Fig. 3A and C). However, the relationship between moderate-intensity METs and sarcopenia revealed an L-shaped nonlinear trend. After stratifying PA by occupational and recreational type, the relationships between occupational moderate- and vigorousintensity PA and sarcopenia showed shapes similar to those of the unstratified relationship, whereas the nonlinear trend became nonsignificant (Fig. 3E and F). passages.heading: **Covariates**
passages.text: The sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, and disease history of the participants were considered covariates in the study. Sociodemographic information included age, sex, marital status (married or unmarried), educational attainment (below high school, above high school), race (Mexican-American, non-Hispanic white, non-Hispanic black, and other races), and socioeconomic status (non-poor: a poverty-to-income ratio equal to one or higher, poor: a poverty-to-income ratio lower than one) [33]. Lifestyle factors included smoking status (non-smoking and smoking), alcohol consumption (not drinking and drinking), as any smoking or alcohol consumption is harmful [34, 35]. Nutritional status was classified into three categories (normal: BMI < 25.0, overweight: BMI = 25.0-29.9, obesity: BMI > 29.9) according to the WHO criteria [8, 36]. However, underweight participants (BMI < 18.5) were combined with those who had a normal weight because of the small proportion of underweight participants in the sample (1.6%). Patients with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, or hyperlipidemia were classified into dichotomous groups (yes, no). Hypertension was determined if the participants had any of the following conditions: (1) systolic blood pressure >= 140 mmHg; (2) diastolic blood pressure >= 90 mmHg; or (3) had been formally diagnosed [33]. Diabetes mellitus was defined if the participants had any of the following conditions: (1) had been formally diagnosed by a physician or were taking anti-diabetes medication (pills or insulin); (2) had a glycemic hemoglobin (HbA1c) >= 6.5%; or (3) had a fasting blood glucose >= 126 mg/dL [37]. Hyperlipidemia was determined if the participants had any of the following conditions: (1) had been formally diagnosed; (2) had total cholesterol >= 200 mg/dL; (3) had triglycerides >= 150 mg/dL; (4) had high-density lipoprotein < 40 mg/dL (for males) or < 50 mg/dL (for females); or (5) had low-density lipoprotein >= 130 mg/dL [38]. Depression was measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), a nineitem instrument that assesses the frequency of depressive symptoms over the past 2 weeks. The continuous total PHQ-9 score (ranging from 0 to 27) was introduced into the regression model [23, 39].

passages.heading: **Statistical analysis**
passages.text: The characteristics of the study population are expressed as the means and standard deviations (SDs) for continuous variables and percentages for categorical variables. For component differences for continuous variables, a t test or ANOVA was used. The chi-square test was used for between-group differences in categorical variables. Binary logistic regression models were used to estimate the association between PA intensity and sarcopenia, and odds ratios (ORs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used to describe these associations. Three models were developed to test the associations: Model 1 was non-adjusted; Model 2 was adjusted only for sex and age; Model 3 was adjusted for race, education, marital status, poverty-to-income ratio, nutritional status, smoking, alcohol consumption, depression, hypertension, diabetes, and hyperlipidemia based on Model 2. Additionally, restricted cubic splines (RCSs) were used to describe the dose-response relationship between PA and sarcopenia incidence through the recommended 3-5 nodes. Fully adjusted RCS models were used to examine the nonlinear relationship between the intensity and occupational nature of PA and sarcopenia [40]. Two methods of sensitivity analysis were used to test the robustness of the results. First, missing covariate data were imputed by using a mode imputation. The results and figures obtained from imputed datasets are presented. Second, the participants were divided into three categories according to their frequency of drinking (never, every day, and not every day), and the variable was introduced into the regression model with other covariates instead of the dichotomous variable (not drinking, drinking). All the statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 25.0 (IBM, USA) and STATA 16.0 (Stata Corp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). Figures were drawn by using R version 4.3.1 and GraphPad Prism 9 software (GraphPad Software Inc., La Jolla, CA, USA). A two-sided p value < 0.05 was considered to indicate statistical significance.

passages.heading: **Study design and data collection**
passages.text: The data for the current study were obtained from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), which is an ongoing study with a multistage design that began in the early 1960s. The NHANES aimed to evaluate the health and nutritional status of Americans, and the findings could be used to determine the prevalence of major diseases and their risk factors. The surveys were conducted every 2 years, and a complex probability sampling method was used to represent the noninstitutionalized population in the United States. Data on sociodemographic characteristics, lifestyle factors, disease history, and various anthropometric measures of the participants were collected by trained interviewers and physicians. The questionnaire we used for the data collection in the current study has been published elsewhere [23]. The study protocols were approved by the National Center for Health Statistics Research Ethics Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent. In the present study, data from 4 cycles of the NHANES (2011 ~ 2012, 2013 ~ 2014, 2015 ~ 2016, and 2017 ~ 2018) were used, with an initial sample of 39,156 participants. Participants who met the following criteria were excluded: (1) were aged younger than 20 years ( _n_ = 16538); (2) had any missing data on dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and body mass index ( _n_ = 11792); (3) had any missing PA information ( _n_ = 54); and (4) had any missing data on other variables that were necessary for data analysis, including smoking status, alcohol consumption, depression, hypertension status, diabetes status, hyperlipidemia status, and the household povertyto-income ratio ( _n_ = 1970). Ultimately, 8802 participants were included in the data analysis in this study (Fig. 1).
